Mathematical formulation: explore then refine: sample the allocation simplex (Dirichlet, adaptive batches), keep the feasible points, run Nelder-Mead from the best few; the objective is normalised by the baseline and penalised on a four-rung feasibility ladder

Reference (verified): Book Chapter 5 discusses optimum staging analytically (pp.286-296); the numerical search is this tool's own
Assumptions: Local optimum within bounds, for a fixed stage count, propellants, diameters and structural model. `cost` means DEVELOPMENT cost: the chapter's cost per flight is a rule of thumb on payload mass and was measured not to vary with the vehicle at all. `payload` maximises payload at the design's own lift-off mass, by bisection
Validity range / limitations: Not a global optimum, and the spread between starts is reported rather than claimed away. A local search ALONE is not sufficient: on examples/example_3stage_leo.yaml the equal split is infeasible, so a search started there returned its own starting point as the answer - which is why the exploration phase exists. With the book's loss models no trajectory quantity enters the objective, so the lightest split can be one that flies badly; with simulated losses (M109) the losses follow the split
Verification: tests/test_optimiser.py: the 3-stage design that defeated the old search is optimised to its known 4.8 % gain; the 2-stage answer is unchanged; a search that finds nothing reports failure instead of a penalty posing as a mass; the sizing loop's seed is swept and the converged answer is invariant to 1e-8

Reference (verified): Book Table 6.1 and Eqs. 6:40-6:43, 6:49-6:53, pp.362-364; gravity turn Sec. 6.4.7 and Eq. 6:58

Validity range / limitations: trajectory.integrate is the pure gravity turn, kept for flying published pitch programmes (tools/validate_drag.py) and the book's shooting method (M65). A design is flown to orbit by M108, which adds steering, cutoff, coasts and the Earth's rotation to these equations. RK4 at 0.25 s
Verification: tests/test_trajectory.py: closure residual, step-size independence, monotonicity in the kick

Mathematical formulation: dv_ideal(vac) = integral T_vac/m dt; gravity = integral g sin(gamma) dt; drag = integral D/m dt; propulsion = integral Ae Pinf/m dt; steering = integral 2T sin^2(alpha/2)/m dt
Reference (verified): Book Eq. 6:58, p.365
Assumptions: The four losses and the burnout speed reconstruct the vacuum ideal exactly, which is the check that they are one integration decomposed rather than four estimates
Validity range / limitations: The losses of the ascent to the first engine cutoff; a coast and second burn are reported beside them. The steering integrand of M108 also holds the yaw that removes the launch site's speed across the orbit plane
Verification: Closure residual < 1e-6 m/s in tests (ground launch, air launch, solids, strap-ons); Titan II's gravity loss falls inside the book's Table 3.4 range

Mathematical formulation: bisection on the kick angle; a flight that ends on the ground is classified by its peak altitude (lofted = kick too small, flat = kick too large)
Reference (verified): Book Sec. 6.4.7 and Fig. 6.18, pp.369-370
Assumptions: Burnout altitude falls monotonically with the kick over the range where the vehicle flies a turn; outside it the classification keeps the bisection pointed the right way
Validity range / limitations: Kick angles are often far below one degree and the trajectory is extremely sensitive to them (the book says so); a result that crosses the target altitude with |gamma| > 10 deg is rejected as not an insertion
Verification: tests/test_trajectory.py: monotonicity, convergence on the target altitude, and honest refusal of an unreachable one

Mathematical formulation: v_ss = (9.5 m/s) h^0.2; effective speed v_R = 2.85 v_ss; q = rho v_R^2/2 at rho = 1.2807 kg/m3; transverse drag D_i = 0.77 q A_side,i applied at each segment's side-area centroid
Outputs [units]: axial, shear and bending distributions on the pad [N, N, N m]
Reference (verified): Book Eqs. 9:20, 9:22, 9:23 and Sec. 9.1.5.1-9.1.5.3, pp.559-562; side areas from Table 9.3, p.555
Assumptions: Steady wind plus vortex shedding and gust lumped into one effective speed; the Eastern Test Range profile; tanks full and unpressurised, which is the critical ground condition the book names; the vehicle is a cantilever, so no inertia relief
Validity range / limitations: Pad height above the ground is an input, because the wind profile is a function of height and a vehicle stands on a launch mount. Strap-on boosters are excluded: they are separate beams
Implementation: loads.ground_wind_case (n_x = 1 clamped, n_x = liftoff T/W for the lift-off case)
Verification: tests/test_loads.py reproduces every side area, wind speed, dynamic pressure and drag force of the book's Saturn V Table 9.5 (p.566) and its shear column to 0.3 %

Calculation / model: Area centroid of a tapering segment
Mathematical formulation: zbar above the aft end = l (2 d_fwd + d_aft) / (3 (d_fwd + d_aft))
Reference (verified): Derived; the book's Table 9.3 cone (l/3) and cylinder (l/2) entries are the two limits of it
Assumptions: The projected side area has width varying linearly between the end diameters, so the centroid is the first moment of that trapezoid; the same expression is the centroid of a slender frustum's normal-force distribution, which also varies as the local radius
Validity range / limitations: Table 9.3's printed skirt entry, l(d1/d3 + 2)/(3(d1/d3 + 1)), is this expression with the two diameters interchanged: it gives 2l/3 rather than l/3 as the forward diameter goes to zero, contradicting the book's own cone entry, and places the centroid on the narrow side of mid-span. The correct form is used here and the difference is quantified against the book's Saturn V tables
Verification: tests/test_loads.py: the cone and cylinder limits, the mirror relationship to the book's expression, and the side on which the centroid must fall

Calculation / model: Flight loads at max-q and max-q alpha
Mathematical formulation: alpha = atan(v_wind/v) from the AMR 95% wind envelope; N_i = CNa alpha q dA_i and D_i = 0.7 q |dA_i| per tapering panel, rotated into body axes by V = L cos(alpha) + D sin(alpha), A = D cos(alpha) - L sin(alpha); gimbal side force from moment balance about the CM; n_z = F_lat/(m g0); inertia relief -n_z m_k g0 at every mass CM; n_x = (T - D)/(m g0)
Outputs [units]: axial, shear and bending distributions in flight [N, N, N m]
Reference (verified): Book Sec. 9.1.6 and the recipe on pp.573-574; Table 9.8, p.596; Sec. 9.2.5; wind fit p.572
Assumptions: Quasi-static trim: the vehicle is balanced at one instant with no attitude dynamics; aerodynamic loads only where the diameter changes, cylinders carrying none to first order (p.577); masses lumped at the ledger's CM positions; apparent weights applied at the aft end of the supporting structure
Validity range / limitations: Max-q, max-q alpha and the instant of greatest axial acceleration are all built, because the book states which governs cannot be known before a trajectory exists (p.572) and lists max axial acceleration among its cases without working it. The axial air load is scaled so its total is the drag the trajectory flew with, which makes n_x consistent with the trajectory and closes the axial curve on the thrust; the book's own example leaves a 3.8 % non-closure by mixing a measured axial force with summed panel estimates
Verification: tests/test_loads.py reproduces the book's Table 9.8 body-axis loads, its gimbal trim (1,161 kN), F_lat (2,736 kN), n_z (0.154) and all eighteen rows of the Table 9.11 axial running total

Calculation / model: Normal force slope of a tapering panel
Mathematical formulation: CNa = 2/rad on the reference area |pi (D^2 - d^2)/4|, with the sign of the area change
Reference (verified): Book Table 9.7, p.578 (subsonic closed form); supersonic charts Figs. 9.38-9.39 NOT reproduced
Assumptions: The slender-body value, which is exactly what the book's subsonic table gives for both a nose cone (2/rad = 0.0349/deg) and a skirt (2(D2^2 - D1^2)/Dref^2). A reverse taper has a negative area change and so a normal force of the opposite sign (p.579)
Validity range / limitations: The book's supersonic charts are digitised plots whose origin the book itself says is unknown, so they are not reproduced. Against their Saturn V reads at M = 1.71 this default under-predicts a nose-cone-plus-afterbody by about 30 % (the chart carries lift over onto the cylinder behind the cone) and over-predicts a flare by 29-67 %. Per-panel chart reads can be supplied through aerodynamics.cna_overrides
Verification: tests/test_loads.py: cylinders carry none, overrides apply by panel name, and a boattail reverses sign

Calculation / model: Normal-force build-up and centre of pressure
Mathematical formulation: CNa_vehicle = sum_i CNa_i A_ref,i / Sref with the sign of the area change; z_cp = sum_i CNa_i A_ref,i z_i / sum_i CNa_i A_ref,i; static margin = (z_cm - z_cp)/D in calibers; Cma = sum_i CNa_i (z_i - z_cm)/L
Outputs [units]: CNa [1/rad], centre of pressure [m], static margin [calibers], Cma [1/rad]
Reference (verified): Book Table 9.7 and Figs. 9.38-9.39 for the panel slopes; stability definition p.357; reference area convention p.358
Assumptions: Each panel's normal force acts at the centroid of its own area change; cylinders carry none to first order (p.577); the CP is independent of angle of attack, which is what the linear CN = CNa alpha assumption means
Validity range / limitations: Omitting the cylinders omits viscous crossflow, which acts mostly aft of the nose, so the CP comes out FURTHER FORWARD than reality and the static margin is pessimistic by an unquantified amount. The slender-body default is Mach-independent, so the CP does not move with speed unless chart reads are supplied. No fins, boosters or protuberances. Where reverse tapers make the total slope pass through zero the CP is meaningless and the module says so; Cma stays defined and is the measure to read
Verification: tests/test_loads.py: the book's own Saturn V force list (Fig. 9.65) gives z_cp = 55.95 m and 2.13 calibers of instability, and removing the fins' 126 kN moves the CP 0.41 calibers forward - which is Sec. 9.2.7's claim that the fins added stability, as a number

Mathematical formulation: pattern (compass) search on hand-over altitude and vertical rise time; objective = the speed in hand at the end of the flight; the steering is solved and the pitch kick searched inside every evaluation
Outputs [units]: optimum programme, loss budget, what stops it
Reference (verified): Book Sec. 6.7 poses the problem and declines to solve it (p.383: the mathematics 'will not be presented here'); Sec. 6.10 states the trade; Fig. 6.26 its shape
Assumptions: Within the flights M108 can fly, not over all possible profiles. The dynamic pressure limit rules out a kick; the q alpha limit bounds the angle between thrust and velocity wherever there is air; the axial limit throttles engines that can
Validity range / limitations: The limits are inputs, not findings: the defaults are what the book's generic vehicle reached, and they decide the answer. With none set the result is the edge of the search box and is reported as meaningless
Verification: tests/test_ascent_opt.py: earlier hand-over lowers gravity loss and raises steering, drag and q alpha (book Sec. 6.10); the search never returns an infeasible point or one worse than its start; every limit can bind alone; the result is deterministic

Mathematical formulation: max over the trajectory of q(t) x |alpha(t)|, in Pa deg
Reference (verified): Book Fig. 9.36, p.572
Assumptions: alpha here is the angle between thrust and velocity, which is zero throughout a pure gravity turn by construction, so q alpha is produced entirely by the steering above it
Validity range / limitations: The book's generic vehicle reaches (q alpha)max = 6,930 lbf deg/ft2 = 331.8 kPa deg, and its max-q 920 lbf/ft2 = 44.0 kPa. Those are the config DEFAULTS and are observed values from one figure, NOT certified limits for any design - they decide the optimisation's answer, so they should be replaced with the vehicle's own
Verification: tests/test_ascent_opt.py: the peak of the product is not the product of the peaks, and a pure gravity turn gives exactly zero

Calculation / model: Payload price of a pitch programme
Mathematical formulation: root-find on added payload mass until the flown vehicle has no speed in hand; everything but lift-off mass frozen
Reference (verified): Book Sec. 6.7 defines the optimum as delivering the largest payload (p.380)
Assumptions: A frozen-vehicle trade: same stages, same propellant loads, same burn times, only the mass at lift-off changes. Both the achieved and the required speed come from the same integration, so no regression enters the comparison
Validity range / limitations: This is what better steering is worth on the vehicle AS BUILT, not what a vehicle designed around the better profile would be - the sizing loop still uses the regression losses, so the optimisation never feeds back into the design
Verification: tests/test_ascent_opt.py: re-flying at the payload the bisection found lands within 30 m/s of the requirement, and a better programme is worth strictly more payload

Calculation / model: Thin-shell stress from axial load and bending
Mathematical formulation: A = 2 pi R t; I = pi R^3 t; sigma_a = P/(2 pi R t); sigma_b = M/(pi R^2 t); sigma_vert = |sigma_a| + |sigma_b| - (p + p_h) R/(2t); sigma_hoop = (p + p_h) R/t; tau = V/(2 pi R t)
Assumptions: Thin wall (t << R), circular section, Bernoulli-Euler bending, stresses uniform around the circumference except for the bending term; the peak compression is taken where axial and bending add
Validity range / limitations: The combined stress state is NOT evaluated - the book sets it aside too ('beyond the scope of this book', p.649). Shear is reported but sizes nothing, following the book's Example 1b where it needs a twentieth of minimum gauge
Verification: tests/test_structure.py reproduces the book's Example 1a exactly: A = 0.007854 m2, I = 0.006136 m4, 195.1 MPa axial, 99.9 MPa bending, 295.0 MPa combined, 28.5 % of the steel allowable and 65.8 % of the aluminium one; Example 1b's shear thicknesses; Example 3a's 215.5 MPa axial and 431 MPa hoop

Mathematical formulation: sigma_c = (K0 + Kp) E t/R with K0 = 9(t/R)^0.6 + 0.16 (R/L)^1.3 (t/R)^0.3 and Kp = min(0.191 (p/E)(R/t)^2, 0.229); equivalently sigma_c/E = 9(t/R)^1.6 + 0.16(t/L)^1.3 unpressurised
Inputs [units]: R, L, t, E, ullage pressure
Reference (verified): Book Eqs. 10.25 and 10.31-10.33, pp.635-643 (after Seifert & Boelter, and Harpoothian)
Assumptions: Monocoque isotropic shell, uniform thickness, no imperfection knockdown beyond what the empirical fit already carries; the hydrostatic term is excluded from the buckling pressure because it vanishes when the tank empties, as the book does in Eq. 10.42
Validity range / limitations: Buckling, not strength, sizes nearly every shell of a monocoque launch vehicle - the book's own example tanks buckle at 288-364 psi, 'hardly anything'. Pressurisation is the one stabilisation that adds no structural mass (Sec. 10.3.2)
Verification: tests/test_structure.py reproduces Example 2 (sigma_c/E of 9.58e-6 and 3.64e-5, giving 1.98 and 2.51 MPa) and Example 3b (K0 of 0.05249 and 0.08630, Kp saturated at 0.229, sigma_c of 10.63 and 9.16 MPa, 5.4x and 3.7x the dry values), and asserts that the two printed forms of the unpressurised criterion are algebraically identical

Mathematical formulation: t_axial = FS/sigma_allow [P/(2 pi R) + M/(pi R^2) - R(p + p_h)/2], floored at zero; t_hoop = FS R (p + p_h)/sigma_allow; t_buckling solves applied = critical by bisection; t = max(all three, minimum gauge) over every load case
Reference (verified): Book Eqs. 10.43-10.46 and Table 10.2, pp.634-654
Assumptions: Each shell is loaded with the largest axial force, shear and moment anywhere along its own length, which may be three different stations - conservative on purpose. Ground cases carry NO tank pressure, which is the book's explicit rule (p.650) and is what makes the pad size the tanks
Validity range / limitations: Eq. 10.43's bracket goes negative when pressure more than cancels the compression; the book reads that correctly in its text but prints the magnitude (0.41 mm) just above. Taking the magnitude would make MORE pressure demand a THICKER wall, inverting the chapter's argument, so the result is floored at zero. Mass is rho x surface area x thickness and is NOT fed back into the vehicle
Verification: tests/test_structure.py reproduces Example 5's 2.14 mm hoop thickness and its negative axial bracket, asserts the buckling root really is a root, and asserts that required thickness falls monotonically with pressure

Mathematical formulation: P/P_cr + M/M_cr = 1 with P_cr = 0.33 (2 pi E t^2 cos^2 a)/sqrt(3(1-mu^2)), M_cr = 0.41 (pi E t^2 r cos^2 a)/sqrt(3(1-mu^2)), a = atan((R-r)/h)
Reference (verified): Book Sec. 10.3.1.1, p.638, quoting NASA SP-8019 'Buckling of Thin-Walled Truncated Cones'
Assumptions: The small end's radius governs, because 'buckling occurs when the max stress near the small end of the cone is equal to the critical compressive stress for a cylinder having the same wall thickness and local radius of curvature'
Validity range / limitations: Reported for tapering segments beside the cylinder criterion rather than replacing it, so both are visible
Verification: tests/test_structure.py: the interaction equation, the semivertex angle, and the cylinder limit at zero taper

Calculation / model: Monocoque mass against the mass relationships
Mathematical formulation: sum over shells of rho x S x t_required, beside the Chapter 8 MER mass for the same hardware
Reference (verified): SUPPLEMENTARY comparison of two methods the book presents separately (Chapter 8 masses, Chapter 10 thicknesses)
Assumptions: Compares only the shells both methods cover; the fairing is excluded because it is a composite sandwich sized by an areal-mass relationship and Chapter 10 gives no sandwich allowables
Validity range / limitations: On the default design the monocoque sizing is about twice the relationship mass. Neither is wrong: the relationships are fitted to real vehicles and real vehicles are stiffened, so the gap is what rings, stringers, waffle and isogrid buy back - the efficiency this analysis cannot model because Sec. 10.3.3 names those concepts without giving allowables. It is NOT a correction to apply to the design
Verification: tests/test_structure.py asserts the ratio exceeds one and that the mass follows rho x area x thickness exactly

Calculation / model: Time to double for an unstable vehicle
Mathematical formulation: T2 = ln(2) sqrt(I_y / M_A), with M_A the destabilising aerodynamic pitching moment about the CM; bandwidth f_b = sqrt(M_A/I_y)/(2 pi)
Reference (verified): Book Eq. 12.4 and Sec. 12.3.6 rules 2 and 9, pp.740, 763
Assumptions: Rigid body, pitch plane, the moment taken as constant over the divergence; meaningless for a stable vehicle, where infinity is returned rather than a complex number
Validity range / limitations: The criterion is T2 > 0.5 s (after Falangas); below it 'very fast actuators are needed'. The book's own Saturn V example prints the finless moment as '37 kNm', which gives 100 s rather than its stated 3.15 s - it must be 37 MN m; and it reads the finless case as giving 'slightly more time' when its own numbers give 160 ms LESS, the direction that matches Sec. 9.2.7's argument for the fins
Verification: tests/test_control.py reproduces the book's 3.31 s for the Saturn V at max-q from its printed inertia and moment, and pins both of the slips above

Calculation / model: Control authority and gimbal deflection budget
Mathematical formulation: M_delta = f T sin(delta_max) l_c; controllability = M_delta/M_A; trim deflection = asin(M_A/(f T l_c)); total deflection = RSS of the trim term with the Table 12.4 contributors
Inputs [units]: thrust, gimbal travel, gimbal-to-CM arm, aerodynamic moment
Reference (verified): Book Sec. 12.3.6 rules 1 and 3, Table 12.4, pp.740-763
Assumptions: Quasi-static trim at each instant; only the steerable share f of the thrust counts (the Saturn V gimballed four of five F-1s); no actuator rate, lag or saturation dynamics
Validity range / limitations: Rules applied: controllability >= 2.0 ('typically > 1, although values less than 1/2 have been observed in Delta III vehicles'), steady-state deflection <= 2 deg. Only the steady-state wind term of the budget is this vehicle's own; the other four are the book's figures for one NASA solid-Saturn study and are stand-ins, not requirements. The totals printed in Table 12.4 are about 13 % above the root-sum-square of its own rows, while its arithmetic totals match them exactly, so the RSS the book defines in words is the one used
Verification: tests/test_control.py reproduces Table 12.4's simultaneous totals exactly (2.40, 3.46, 2.20 deg), pins the RSS discrepancy, and checks that trim deflection and control moment are inverses

Mathematical formulation: Pc = [rho a c* (A_b/A_t)]^(1/(1-n)), assembled from r = a Pc^n, mdot = rho A_b r and c* = Pc A_t/mdot
Reference (verified): Book Eq. 4:32 and Eq. 4:33, p.231-232, with Table 4.4, p.228
Assumptions: Equilibrium at every instant (no ignition or tail-off transient, no chamber filling dynamics); the exponent 1/(1-n) is the book's own stability argument and n >= 1 is refused rather than solved
Validity range / limitations: Eq. 4:32 is printed as 'mdot = a Pc^b', but the surrounding text introduces it as the law for the BURN RATE and its 0.4-0.7 exponent is the burning-rate exponent; taken literally beside Eq. 4:33 it would give two different expressions for the same mdot. It is read here as r = a Pc^n, which is de Saint Robert's law as universally written and the only reading consistent with Eq. 4:33
Verification: tests/test_internal_ballistics.py asserts that at the solved pressure the propellant produces exactly as much gas as the throat passes, which is all three relations closing on each other, and that n >= 1 raises rather than returns

Mathematical formulation: A_b(w) = -dV/dw of the cast grain with the bore at R_bore + w; end burner A_b = pi R_int^2
Assumptions: Uniform regression normal to the burning surface; computed from the same grain-volume function the motor was sized with, so geometry and ballistics cannot disagree. For a bore through the barrel it reduces to 2 pi (R_bore + w) h_cyl
Validity range / limitations: Only the two shapes the book describes completely are offered: the end burner (neutral) and the hollow cylinder (progressive, which the book states will 'produce thrust levels that increase with time'). The star, cog and finocyl grains of Fig. 4.12 are drawn but never dimensioned, so their burning-area laws are not in this book and are not invented
Verification: tests/test_internal_ballistics.py: the core-burn area matches the analytic bore surface, the end burner is exactly neutral, and the cylindrical grain is progressive as the book says

Calculation / model: Burning-rate coefficient calibration and thrust profile
Mathematical formulation: a solved from Pc_design = [rho a c* A_b_mean/A_t]^(1/(1-n)); then Pc(w), r(w), mdot(w), F(w) and t(w) = integral dw/r
Inputs [units]: sized motor, propellant n and c*
Reference (verified): SUPPLEMENTARY calibration of book Eqs. 4:32-4:33
Assumptions: The book gives no burning-rate coefficient for any propellant - they are 'experimentally measured propellant characteristics that vary among propellants' (p.231) - so rather than inventing one, a is solved for from the motor the sizing already produced. The curves are therefore a statement about the GRAIN SHAPE, not about a propellant this tool has no data for
Validity range / limitations: Because a plain cylindrical grain is strongly progressive, the delivered burn time and total impulse differ from the sized ones and the peak chamber pressure runs well past the design value - on the example vehicle by a factor of 1.9, which the casing was not sized for. That mismatch is the finding, not an error to reconcile: it says the constant-thrust assumption behind the sizing needs a shaped grain the book does not dimension. Nothing is re-sized from it
Verification: tests/test_internal_ballistics.py: the calibration reproduces the design pressure exactly, mass flow and thrust are consistent at every point, the reported impulse is the trapezoid of its own curve, and a propellant without n or c* is refused rather than guessed

Mathematical formulation: H = a M^x f1 f2 f3 f8 in work-years: H_ES = 16.3 M^0.54 (solid motors), H_EL = 277 M^0.48 (turbopump engines), H_EP = 167 M^0.35 (pressure-fed engines), H_VR = 10.4 M^0.60 (solid boosters), H_VS = 100 M^0.555 (stage dry mass without engines); programme = f0 x sum, f0 = 1.04^N stages
Inputs [units]: one engine's mass, stage dry mass without engines (with fairing and adapter on the first liquid stage), motor or booster net mass; f1, f2, f3, region, what is already developed
Reference (verified): Book Eq. 17.3 and Figs. 17.12-17.16, pp.998-1005, Table 17.4; Koelle, Handbook of Cost Engineering, TCS-TR-184 (TRANSCOST 7.2), 2007, pp.21, 28-32, 34, 37, 40, 42, 47, 52-55, 92, 104; work-year values Koelle Table 1-II, p.19, and book Table 17.3; inflation book Eq. 17.1
Assumptions: Top-down and mass-driven, for government programmes run conventionally; Koelle puts commercial developments at 20 to 50 % of it (pp.94-95). f2 of a liquid stage is computed from its net mass fraction against reference curves read off Koelle Figs. 2-28 and 2-29 (about 5 %); below the curves f2 = 1. Solid stages use ES; strap-ons use VR from 10 t net and ES below, because VR's data start at 11 t (SUPPLEMENTARY choice)
Validity range / limitations: f1 = f3 = 1 unless set, and they dominate the answer: the ten engines of Koelle Fig. 2-09 scatter from 0.66 to 2.0 of the bare relation. The book's Table 17.4 is a misprinted copy of Koelle Table 2-V: it drops the shroud and equipment-bay masses and misprints the SRB's CER value and the core's f1. Not included: agency cost, schedule slips, flight tests beyond the first
Implementation: cost.CERS / element_effort_wyr / estimate, the Cost tab
Verification: tests/test_cost.py: Koelle's Ariane 5 (five rows and the 40,827 total), SSME and SSTO-engine examples reproduce; tools/validate_cost.py measures sized vehicles against real programmes (docs/COST_VALIDATION.md)

Mathematical formulation: WYr/Mg = 110 M^-0.387 for LEO payload M in Mg; payload mass x $5,000 per pound; real prices and work-years from Table 17.5
Reference (verified): Book Sec. 17.5.3, p.995; Fig. 17.17, p.1008, and Table 17.5, pp.1010-1011; the fit itself is SUPPLEMENTARY
Assumptions: The fit is to the 19 vehicles of Table 17.5 that state work-years per flight and a LEO payload, without Saturn and Shuttle; the book gives the scatter about its own line as +100 %/-50 % (p.1009)
Validity range / limitations: Shown beside the estimate, never mixed into it. For LEO payloads only. Prices are in their own currency and are not converted
Verification: tests/test_cost.py: the fit is recomputed from the table

Mathematical formulation: first unit F = a M^x: 2.3 M^0.399 (solid motors and boosters, with propellant), 5.16 M^0.45 (LH2 engines), 1.9 M^0.535 (other engines), 1.30 M^0.65 (LH2 stages), 0.83 M^0.65 (other liquid stages); vehicle = 1.025^N x sum(n F f4) f8; f4 = mean of k^(ln p/ln 2) over the units built
Inputs [units]: element masses, engines and boosters per vehicle, launches per year, flights
Reference (verified): Koelle, Handbook of Cost Engineering, TCS-TR-184 (TRANSCOST 7.2), 2007, pp.118-120, 124-125, 129-130, 133-134, 140-141
Assumptions: f0 per stage is between 1.02 and 1.03 (p.124) and 1.025 is used. p is read off Figs. 3-07 and 3-15 against unit mass and yearly rate
Validity range / limitations: Historical complexity: Koelle puts the RS-68 more than 50 % below the engine relation (p.128). Liquid strap-ons are costed as a stage with the engine inside. No reuse
Verification: tests/test_cost.py: Koelle's five S-II stages (4,515) and F-1 engine (139.1) reproduce, and the learning-chart readings against his worked values

Calculation / model: Ground, mission and indirect operations cost
Mathematical formulation: ground = 8 M0^0.67 L^-0.9 N^0.7 fv fc f4 f8; mission = 20 sum(Q) L^-0.65 f4 f8; cost per flight = (production + ground + mission)/(1 - 0.115)
Inputs [units]: launch mass [Mg], launches per year, stages and boosters, assembly mode, flights
Reference (verified): Koelle, Handbook of Cost Engineering, TCS-TR-184 (TRANSCOST 7.2), 2007, pp.157-158, 164, 180
Assumptions: Koelle calls both operations CERs provisional. 0.115 is the middle of his 8 to 15 % for the indirect share. Operations learning 0.90, the middle of his 0.85-0.95, and only from 6 launches a year
Validity range / limitations: Propellants, transport, insurance, fees and profit are left out. Against 13 vehicles of Koelle's price tables the cost per flight has a median ratio of 1.73 and only one is within 20 % (docs/COST_VALIDATION.md)
Verification: tests/test_cost.py: the parts recomputed by hand for the default vehicle; tools/validate_cost.py

Mathematical formulation: per flight event: axial from the trajectory's n_x = (T-D)/(m g0), lateral from the Chapter 9 flight trim n_z; design factor = worst (static + dynamic) over all events
Reference (verified): Book Sec. 11.4 and Tables 11.3-11.4, pp.690-692
Source class: Book (format and ranges) + SUPPLEMENTARY (the vehicle's own numbers)
Assumptions: The steady half is computed; the DYNAMIC half is not. A published QSL is the worst combination of dynamic and steady acceleration and the dynamic part comes from a coupled-loads analysis of vehicle and spacecraft together, which needs structural modes this tool does not compute - so the increments are taken from the two real guides the book prints and are stand-ins
Validity range / limitations: The book's expectation for a preliminary design is 4-8 g axial and 1.5-3 g lateral (p.691). No acoustic or shock specification is produced: Chapter 11 describes ignition overpressure, lift-off acoustics, buffet and pyrotechnic shock without a prediction method for any ('difficult to estimate', p.676). No frequency requirement either - Sec. 11.5.3 asks for spacecraft modes at twice the vehicle's, and the vehicle's are not computed
Verification: tests/test_payload_env.py: the generated factors land inside the book's typical ranges, the worst axial falls on a burnout as both real guides show, and every missing piece of a real guide is asserted to be declared rather than filled

Calculation / model: Declared trade study and design comparison
Mathematical formulation: every case is a full sizing run with the declared parameter overrides applied to the design dictionary; results tabulated side by side
Inputs [units]: a YAML sweep declaration or a list of designs
Reference (verified): SUPPLEMENTARY tooling; no book method
Assumptions: Nothing is recomputed: every output is the sizing loop's own, so a trade carries exactly the assumptions and warnings a single-design run does
Validity range / limitations: Cases that fail to converge or violate a constraint stay in the results table rather than being dropped, and one unreadable file or bad parameter path costs its own row only. A trade whose spread is smaller than the MER uncertainty (tens of per cent on GLOM) is telling you about the model rather than the vehicles, and the report says so
Verification: tests/test_studies.py: every combination is run, a 3.6 m stage-1 case fails on ENGFIT and survives into the table, an unknown parameter path fails one case not the run, and the swept parameter is asserted to have actually moved the vehicle

Mathematical formulation: the sized segment list is reduced to a (z, r) profile, then revolved about the axis into closed triangle meshes - one for the airframe, one per nozzle and one per strap-on - and written as STL, OBJ and 3MF; the same profile is drawn as a layered DXF R12 inboard profile
Outputs [units]: DXF profile, STL, OBJ and 3MF meshes [m]
Reference (verified): SUPPLEMENTARY tooling; no book method
Assumptions: A conceptual outer mould line, not a solid model of hardware: the parts are not booleaned into one solid (that needs a CAD kernel), they overlap where a nozzle sits inside an aft skirt, and a revolved surface is polygonal, so its volume falls short of the true body of revolution by about 0.16 % at the default 64 facets
Validity range / limitations: 3MF is the one to prefer over STL: identical triangles, but it records the UNIT its coordinates are in and keeps one named object per part, where STL records neither and fuses every part into one anonymous shell. No STEP is written by this method - exact solids are M92, through an optional kernel. What is delivered here is checked without any dependency: each part's mesh volume against the closed-form volume of a faceted solid of revolution, every edge shared by exactly two oppositely-wound triangles, the 3MF unzipped and re-parsed against the 3MF Core Specification's structure, winding, index-base and unit rules by a reader written from that specification, and the DXF parsed back with an independent group-code reader. None of that is a substitute for opening the files in a CAD application, which has not been done
Implementation: cad_export.core_profile / revolve / write_stl / write_obj / write_3mf / write_dxf
Verification: tests/test_cad_export.py: exact faceted volumes for prism, cone and stepped profiles, watertightness with a deliberately broken mesh to prove the check can fail, STL and OBJ parsed back and compared triangle by triangle, and the DXF silhouette checked against the geometry it came from

Mathematical formulation: a declared sheet of published figures is mapped onto the annotated design schema; every imported leaf is tagged t = reference with its own source string and everything else keeps the base design's value and tag
Inputs [units]: a CSV or JSON vehicle sheet, or Wikipedia infobox wikitext
Outputs [units]: an annotated design YAML plus an import report
Reference (verified): SUPPLEMENTARY tooling; no book method
Assumptions: An import supplies only what sources publish - payload to a stated orbit, diameters, engine counts, thrust, Isp, propellants. Stage dry and propellant masses, tankage, pressures, materials and engine envelopes are not published and stay at the base design's assumed values, which is precisely why the result is a validation case and not a datasheet
Validity range / limitations: Two findings drive the design. First, cloning a stage template across size classes carries ABSOLUTE mass assumptions that do not scale: the default 10 t-class base contributes 100 kg of equipment, 60 kg of separation hardware and 25 kg per engine of feed system per stage, which roughly doubles an Electron-sized vehicle's inert mass - so the report warns whenever the payload masses differ by more than 3x and names every carried leaf. Second, Wikipedia infoboxes cannot be imported blind: a single cell routinely holds several vehicle variants, so any field that does not reduce to one figure is refused and listed as ambiguous rather than guessed. launchercalculator.com, named in the roadmap, turned out to be a calculator with no published dataset at all
Verification: tests/test_vehicle_import.py: the shipped example sheet is imported, sized and compared against the hand-written validation cases for the same vehicles (Falcon 9 lands 8 % heavy, Electron 17 %), missing required fields and unknown or mistyped columns raise rather than defaulting, and the infobox parser is shown refusing Falcon 9's multi-variant mass and height cells

Mathematical formulation: a library of oxidiser/fuel pairs carrying two mixture ratios - the Isp optimum and what engines actually fly - plus reference Isp, c*, chamber temperature and mixture specific gravity; bulk density recomputed as (1+r)/(r/rho_ox + 1/rho_fuel)
Outputs [units]: mixture ratio [-], bulk density [kg/m3], density impulse [N s/m3]
Reference (verified): Book Table 4.10 (p.240) for seven combinations, Table 4.5 (p.238) for methane and propane, cited papers for the two peroxide pairs
Assumptions: The reference Isp is theoretical at the book's condition - 1,000 psia expanded optimally to sea level - so it is NOT a vacuum Isp and is never filled into a stage; a large-area-ratio vacuum nozzle legitimately beats it (RD-180 delivers 338 s against Table 4.10's 300 s for LOX/RP-1). Only the mixture ratio and the propellant names are filled. The peroxide rows are at their own sources' conditions and are not comparable with the book rows
Validity range / limitations: Two mixture ratios are carried deliberately: engines do not run at peak Isp, and for LOX/LH2 the gap is 4.02 against the J-2's flown 5.50. The transcription is checked by recomputing each Table 4.10 row's printed specific gravity from the component densities and its own mixture ratio - six of seven agree inside 2 %, the exception being the 75 %-ethanol row whose fuel is denser than the pure ethanol in the library. That same identity CONFIRMS INDEPENDENTLY that Table 4.6's Aerozine-50 density is a misprint: 1.21 is reachable from 903 kg/m3 and not from the 1,450 kg/m3 printed, which duplicates the N2O4 row above it
Verification: tests/test_propellant_combinations.py: the S.G. identity across every book row, the Aerozine-50 misprint shown both ways, Table 4.5 checked against Table 4.10 through the reciprocal, and the fill rules (stage wins, contradictions warned, solid stages refused)

Calculation / model: Winds aloft from the launch site's own data
Mathematical formulation: a profile of wind speed against altitude read from CSV or Excel replaces the book's Atlantic Missile Range curve; gust speed at the condition's altitude gives alpha = atan(v_wind/v), which selects the instant and sets the angle of attack for the flight load cases
Inputs [units]: a wind profile file, or the built-in book curve
Reference (verified): Book Sec. 9.1.6.3 step 4 and Fig. 9.35, pp.572-573
Source class: Book (method and default curve) + SUPPLEMENTARY (reading a site's own data)
Assumptions: Horizontal wind only, applied as an instantaneous gust at one altitude - there is no wind in the trajectory integration, so the vehicle is not flown through the profile and the angle of attack is imposed on a state the trajectory reached without it. Direction and shear rate are read if present but not used: the load is built from speed alone
Validity range / limitations: Steady wind and gust envelope are kept as DIFFERENT inputs, because conflating them halves or doubles the design load. The book's AMR curve is a 95-percentile envelope that already contains the gust and is fed straight in; a sounding or a mean profile is steady wind that the gust rides on top of, so a profile declared `steady` REQUIRES an explicit gust increment and is refused without one rather than having a number invented for it. One profile is not a design wind either: several can be given and are flown as an ensemble, and because the worst wind and the worst load are at different altitudes for different vehicles, the case kept is the one that bends the vehicle hardest, not the one with the fastest wind. Every kept case records which profile produced it and the report lists what it was chosen from
Implementation: wind.read_csv / read_excel / book_profile / load, loads.winds_aloft_mps / gust_alpha_rad / standard_cases
Verification: tests/test_wind.py: the book curve reproduced at its own figure's points, unit and column-name variants, a steady profile refused without a gust increment, an ensemble keeping the governing load rather than the governing wind, and the result shown to be independent of the order the profiles are given in

Calculation / model: Exact-solid CAD export through an optional geometry kernel
Mathematical formulation: the same (z, r) meridian as M88 is closed back down the axis and revolved a full turn by CadQuery/OpenCASCADE into an exact B-rep solid per part - exact cylinders and cones, not facets - assembled into a named, coloured tree and written as STEP, BREP or glTF
Inputs [units]: vehicle geometry; a CadQuery installation the user provides
Reference (verified): SUPPLEMENTARY tooling; no book method
Assumptions: OPTIONAL and absent by default: nothing else in the tool depends on it, and without it the M88 exports are written unchanged. It removes the facet deficit (0.161 % of volume at 64 facets) and gives geometry that can be sectioned and measured, but it is still the outer mould line - the parts are not booleaned together and still overlap where a nozzle sits inside an aft skirt. It is asked only for formats M88 cannot write: re-exporting STL or 3MF through the kernel would be duplication, since these meridians are piecewise linear and --cad-facets already controls the only curvature there is
Validity range / limitations: NO CALL IN THIS METHOD HAS EVER REACHED A REAL OPENCASCADE KERNEL. CadQuery is not installable in the environment it was written in (no network), so the module cannot be tested against the thing it drives. Instead of shipping that uncertainty it verifies itself at RUN TIME on the user's machine: every solid's volume as the kernel reports it is compared against a closed-form frustum sum computed with no kernel involved, and against the bounding box the profile implies, and a part out by more than 1e-6 relative means NOTHING IS WRITTEN - the export raises. A wrong API convention therefore fails loudly rather than producing a plausible STEP file with wrong geometry in it. --verify-kernel prints the comparison part by part. Until someone has run it on a real install, STEP and BREP are UNPROVEN
Verification: tests/test_cad_kernel.py: driven against a stub that computes each revolved volume by Pappus' theorem from the points and axis actually passed, so a wrong axis, a dropped offset or a mangled meridian disagrees with the frustum sum; a deliberately wrong axis is shown to be REJECTED with nothing written; the export adapter is shown coping with each documented CadQuery API spelling; an exporter that writes an empty file is shown to be treated as a failure; and the file's own docstring records that a stub is not OpenCASCADE

Mathematical formulation: the whole inert mass of a solid stage from a regression over flown stages, m_i = a m_p (+ b, or a m_p^c), replacing the book's motor-level casing MER and suppressing the component build-up it would otherwise sit on top of
Reference (verified): Zandbergen (TU Delft, 2026) 17 steel + 17 composite flight stages; Kibbey (NASA MSFC, NTRS 20190027424) size-dependent form
Assumptions: Every relation here predicts a STAGE inert mass - casing, skirts, interstage, avionics, the lot - where the book's Eq. 8:18 predicts a MOTOR. Selecting one therefore switches off the bottom-up build-up rather than adding to it, because adding skirts to a number that already contains them is the error this replaces. The relations are regressions over 34 stages with a mean absolute error of 16-20 %, not physics, and as of v0.26 kibbey_medium is the DEFAULT for a composite-cased stage, chosen on measurement: across the 16 published solid stages at their published propellant loads it gives mean absolute stage-inert error 23 % and median bias -8 %, against 51 % and +52 % for the book's flat composite constant. A STEEL case keeps book_steel, because the material matters more than the fitting form - kibbey_medium is 45-49 % light on Ariane 5's segmented-steel EAP and Scout's Algol, where the book's steel k is within -2 % to +5 %. One relation is applied to every composite stage rather than a technology band chosen per vehicle, which after seeing the errors would be indistinguishable from fitting. star_motor measures as well but is fitted to 25-4,300 kg motors and is not used outside that range. The book's methods all stay available and stay reported
Validity range / limitations: The finding that motivated this: the book's COMPOSITE casing coefficient, k = 0.1154, is a motor-level figure as large as the measured STAGE-level fraction of real composite-cased stages (0.111). Everything the tool adds on top then overshoots, and because sizing is a fixed point a 39 % heavy casing made Vega 122 % heavy. Switching to the published relation takes Pegasus XL from +59.6 % to -4.1 % and Epsilon from +58.4 % to -10.4 % against their published lift-off masses. Vega still ends +11.8 %, because its remaining error is a DIFFERENT relation - the book's two-value avionics step puts 280 kg on AVUM, whose real dry mass is 147 kg. NASA's own size-dependent parameters (Kibbey) turn out to under-predict these 34 flown stages by 22-58 %, which is recorded rather than smoothed over
Verification: tests/test_solid_inert.py: every published coefficient is REFITTED from the source's own tabulated stages and reproduced (the steel proportional one exactly, at 0.1707), which is also how an ambiguous printed constant was resolved as tonnes rather than kilograms; the double-count suppression is checked component by component; and the Pegasus and Epsilon results above are asserted

Calculation / model: Engine-cluster reliability and the engine-out case
Mathematical formulation: R_s = sum(j=k..n) C(n,j) R^j (1-R)^(n-j) for a cluster of n engines of which k must work, beside the thrust-to-weight the stage retains with one engine shut down
Inputs [units]: engine count, per-engine reliability, stage thrust and ignition mass
Reference (verified): Book Sec. 15.2.6 (pp.934-937), Table 15.4 (p.936) flight statistics
Assumptions: A cluster calculation over one per-engine number, assuming the engines fail independently. They do not: a shared feed system, a shared controller, or debris from the engine that failed are common-cause failures this does not model, so the result is an upper bound and is reported as one. Nothing here feeds back into sizing
Validity range / limitations: Two things are added to what the book prints. First, Table 15.4 reports two engines as 100 % reliable on records of 0/207 and 0/65; no finite record shows a reliability of 1, so the exact Clopper-Pearson lower bound is reported beside the point estimate (98.6 % and 95.5 % at 95 % confidence). Second, redundancy is only CREDITED where the stage can still fly with an engine shut down - a 9-engine first stage that cannot lift off on 8 has none, whatever the binomial says. The book's own pair of worked examples makes the governing point, that 7-of-9 (99.164 %) is worse than 3-of-5 (99.88 %) at the same per-engine reliability
Verification: tests/test_reliability.py: both of the book's worked examples are reproduced to their printed digits, the zero-failure bound is checked against its closed form (1-c)^(1/n), and the default design's claim that six engines give one-engine-out margin is tested rather than believed

Calculation / model: Measurement of the engine-mass MER against real engines
Mathematical formulation: book Table 8.9 row 1 evaluated for every database engine that publishes a dry mass, with the residual reported per engine and the decision whether to refit made on whether that residual is structured or scattered
Inputs [units]: engine database rows with a published dry mass
Reference (verified): SUPPLEMENTARY (measurement of a book method)
Assumptions: Ten engines is a small sample and two of them are known outliers. It measures the relation; it does not replace it
Validity range / limitations: THE OUTCOME WAS TO CHANGE NOTHING in the relation. Across ten engines the mean error is -7 % but the standard deviation is 45 %, and the trend with engine size (+15 %) is smaller than that scatter - so a refit on this sample would fit noise. What DID change is the uncertainty study: the 1-sigma on engine mass was an assumed 0.15 and is now the measured 0.45, tagged t: reference. The two outliers are the engines the book itself explains - the RS-68 is 55 % heavier than the relation because of its ablative nozzle, the Merlin 1D 104 % lighter because it has the highest thrust-to-weight ever flown
Verification: tests/test_engine_db.py: the verdict is asserted to be SCATTERED, the size trend is asserted smaller than the scatter, the declared 1-sigma is asserted to equal the measurement, and every liquid engine must be either measured or listed with the reason it could not be

Calculation / model: Does a jettisoned item reenter, or stay in orbit
Mathematical formulation: the planet-relative separation state is turned inertial by adding the surface speed omega r cos(lat) east, and the osculating perigee follows from the specific energy and angular momentum: a = -mu/(2 eps), e = sqrt(1 + 2 eps h^2/mu^2), r_p = a(1-e)
Inputs [units]: separation altitude, planet-relative speed, flight path angle, latitude, launch azimuth
Outputs [units]: inertial speed [m/s], perigee and apogee altitude [m], fate
Reference (verified): SUPPLEMENTARY (two-body, applied to the trajectory's own output)
Assumptions: Osculating two-body at the instant of separation: no drag, no J2, no further thrust. The 100 km perigee that separates 'reenters' from 'stays up' is a declared convention, not a physical threshold
Validity range / limitations: This exists because of the failure it prevents. The trajectory integrates a PLANET-RELATIVE speed; an orbit is inertial. Omitting the rotation term makes every upper stage look suborbital, and the tool then invents an impact point for a stage that is actually in orbit - on the reference design the second stage separates at 7,346 m/s relative, which is 7,780 m/s inertial and a 399 km perigee. An item above the threshold is reported as an orbital-lifetime question, which this tool does not model, and is given no impact point at all
Verification: tests/test_debris.py: a circular-orbit state at the pole (where the rotation term vanishes) returns its own altitude as both perigee and apogee; the eastward and westward cases are asserted to gain and lose exactly omega r cos(lat); a 2.9 km/s first stage is required to come down and a 7.35 km/s release at 400 km to stay up; an escape state returns no perigee rather than a nonsense one

Mathematical formulation: the ascent equations of motion (book Table 6.1) integrated with thrust set to zero and the item's own mass and frontal area: dv/dt = -D/m - g sin(gamma), dgamma/dt = -(g/v - v/(Rp+h)) cos(gamma), RK4, to h = 0
Inputs [units]: separation state, item mass [kg] and diameter [m], drag coefficient
Outputs [units]: impact downrange [m], fall time [s], impact speed [m/s], ballistic coefficient [kg/m2]
Reference (verified): Book Table 6.1 equations of motion, p.364, with thrust zero
Assumptions: A single intact body: no breakup, no wind, no lift, no Coriolis, and a constant drag coefficient rather than a Mach-dependent vehicle curve - a tumbling stage does not have one. The same atmosphere as the ascent, so the descent is consistent with the trajectory that produced it rather than being a second model with its own biases
Validity range / limitations: The dominant uncertainty is NOT the one it looks like. Sweeping the drag coefficient of the reference first stage from 0.9 to 2.8, the whole range between flying nose-first and tumbling broadside, moves the impact point 12 km out of 1,084 - about 1 % - because nearly all the downrange is covered on a vacuum coast and drag acts only in the last tens of kilometres, where it is spent on vertical speed. The same sweep changes the impact SPEED from 3,208 m/s (no drag) to 104 m/s. Position is insensitive to drag; velocity is not
Verification: tests/test_debris.py: a vertical drop in near-vacuum reproduces the closed form sqrt(2h/g) to within the step size and travels no downrange; more drag is asserted to give a shorter range, a slower impact and a longer fall; a light wide item is asserted to land slower than a dense one; a zero-mass item is refused rather than dividing by zero

Calculation / model: Impact-point dispersion, and when there is no impact point to give
Mathematical formulation: every corner of a declared uncertainty box - separation speed +/- a fraction, flight path angle +/- an angle, drag over a bracket - is flown down and the along-track interval is the spread; each corner is first tested for orbital energy by M96, and the item is reported NOT LOCALISABLE if any corner is orbital or the spread exceeds a quarter of the Earth's circumference
Outputs [units]: along-track interval [m], drag-only and state-only spreads [m], leverage [m per % of speed]
Reference (verified): SUPPLEMENTARY; no book method
Assumptions: THE DISPERSION INPUTS ARE ASSUMPTIONS, NOT SIGMAS. The defaults (3 % of separation speed, 1 degree of flight path angle) stand in for the guidance and performance dispersions a real analysis gets by Monte Carlo over the actual flight software; nothing in this tool derives them. There is no cross-range at all - a pitch-plane trajectory has no out-of-plane state - so the WIDTH of every hazard area is stated by the user, never computed
Validity range / limitations: What sets the size of a hazard area is how well the vehicle's performance is known, not the drag: for the reference first stage the separation-state assumption accounts for 143 km of the interval and the entire drag bracket for 12 km, and 1 % of separation speed moves the impact point about 20 km. That puts drop zones downstream of the mass model - a solid vehicle carrying the 33 % lift-off-mass error of docs/ACCURACY.md has its drop zones uncertain by a hundred kilometres or more. The not-localisable case is the one that would otherwise produce nonsense: Vega C's third stage separates near orbital speed, its fast corner never reenters, and integrating it anyway yields a hazard area 36,000 km long
Verification: tests/test_debris.py: the claim that the separation state dominates the drag bracket is asserted against the code rather than only stated in prose; a near-orbital release is asserted to come back NOT LOCALISABLE with no window; the corridor half-width is asserted to floor at the Coriolis cross-range the descent omits

Calculation / model: Impact coordinates and hazard-area polygons on a sphere
Mathematical formulation: the direct problem of spherical geodesy: from the pad, walk the downrange arc along the great circle whose initial bearing is the launch azimuth; sin(phi2) = sin(phi1) cos(d) + cos(phi1) sin(d) cos(theta), with each corridor built by stepping perpendicular to the LOCAL course at stations along that arc
Inputs [units]: launch site latitude and longitude, launch azimuth, downrange interval, corridor half-width
Outputs [units]: impact latitude/longitude [deg], ground track and area polygons, KML / GeoJSON
Reference (verified): Standard spherical geodesy; azimuth from M06
Assumptions: A sphere of the same 6,378 km equatorial radius the trajectory integrates with, so the arc produced and the arc walked are the same arc. One great circle, so the ground track does not bend: real ascents dog-leg and yaw-steer. The width of a corridor is an input, never a result
Validity range / limitations: A great-circle arc on this sphere differs from the WGS84 geodesic by up to about half a percent of its length, roughly 5 km at a 1,000 km downrange, and every exported feature carries its own sphere_error_m. A LONGITUDE IS NEEDED FOR COORDINATES AND FOR NOTHING ELSE: a latitude alone fixes all of the physics but not the meridian, so a design that names no launch site still gets its downrange distances and is told plainly why there is no map, rather than silently defaulting to Greenwich. Every exported area carries, in its own description field, the statement that its width is an assumption and that it is not a range-safety product, so the caveat travels with the geometry rather than staying in the documentation
Implementation: geodesy.destination / track / corridor_polygon / position_error_m, hazard.areas / to_kml / to_geojson
Verification: tests/test_geodesy.py and tests/test_hazard.py: closed-form cases where the answer is known without trusting the formula (a quarter circumference due east from the equator, due north reaching the pole, one degree of arc per degree of latitude); the direct and inverse problems are asserted to invert each other to within a metre; the antimeridian is asserted to wrap; corridor points are asserted to sit at the stated half-width; the KML is parsed and every placemark and caveat checked

Calculation / model: Structural material library and a common allowable basis
Mathematical formulation: sigma_allow = 0.633 x published minimum 0.2 % yield, applied identically to every material in the library, with the yield it came from recorded beside it
Outputs [units]: allowable membrane stress [Pa], density [kg/m3], E [Pa], Poisson, CTE [1/K]
Reference (verified): AMS 5519 (301 full hard), AMS 4911 (Ti-6Al-4V), mill datasheets for 304L and 2219-T87
Assumptions: NONE OF THESE IS A QUALIFIED ALLOWABLE. The 0.633 knockdown is a single number standing in for temperature, weld softening beyond the joint efficiency, fatigue, fracture control, and the difference between a specified minimum property and a design allowable. The library is isotropic metals only: no composite is offered, because treating a filament-wound laminate as isotropic would be a modelling lie rather than an approximation
Validity range / limitations: The knockdown exists to make a TRADE honest, not to be right in absolute terms. It is the fraction the original Al-2219 entry already implied (250 MPa against a 395 MPa minimum yield), and it is applied unchanged to every material added since, because quoting one candidate at full yield and another at two thirds of it decides a material trade by bookkeeping. The materials also only reach the mass budget through the pressure_vessel tank method: the Akin relationships are functions of propellant mass or tank volume and never read a material, so a MATUNUSED warning fires when a design names one its own method ignores - otherwise switching aluminium for steel moves lift-off mass by hundredths of a percent and the tool looks broken
Verification: tests/test_gui_robustness.py: every entry is asserted to record the yield its allowable was derated from and to sit within 0.55-0.70 of it; with pressure_vessel sizing the four materials are asserted to order as Ti < Al < 304L, with annealed 304L more than 50 % heavier than aluminium, which is what a seventh of the allowable has to produce

Calculation / model: Actionable refusal: the field at fault and the ways out, solved
Mathematical formulation: when a solid casing cannot hold its propellant, V_case < 2 dome_volume(R), the two remedies are solved exactly rather than described: R_max = cbrt(3 AR V_case / (4 pi)) for the diameter, and m_p_min = rho (4 pi R^3 / (3 AR)) / factor for the propellant
Outputs [units]: the widest feasible diameter [m], the minimum propellant at this diameter [kg], the dotted path of the input at fault
Reference (verified): SUPPLEMENTARY; no book method
Assumptions: Only errors whose cause IS a single input can name one. Where the remedy is not a direct input - propellant mass follows from the delta-v split - the option is offered as advice and explicitly marked as something the user must do themselves rather than a value the tool can set
Validity range / limitations: A message that says 'reduce the diameter or add propellant' is only useful to someone who already knows which diameter and by how much. Solving both ways out turns the refusal into a choice: the diameter becomes a value a user interface sets in one click, the propellant becomes a sentence explaining why it cannot. The structured parts survive being wrapped by SizingError, which is where they used to be lost
Verification: tests/test_gui_robustness.py applies the suggested diameter and asserts the design then sizes - the suggestion has to be correct, not merely present - and asserts every option carries both a label and a reason

Calculation / model: Launch vehicle family: variants of one shared core
Mathematical formulation: a family.yaml manifest names a base design, a reference variant and two or more variants; each variant is the BASE plus dotted-path overrides (boosters.n_total, boosters.n_ground_lit, mission.payload_mass_kg), never a copy, so a shared core is shared structurally; published figures per variant carry {v,u,d,s,t} and must be marked reference; size_family sizes each variant on its own with the delta-v split re-optimised, pinned_family pins the reference variant and asks it for each variant's booster count
Inputs [units]: a family folder with a manifest
Outputs [units]: per-variant GLOM and payload against the published figures, both ways
Reference (verified): SUPPLEMENTARY; the shape is how real launchers are sold, the measurement is this project's
Assumptions: The variants must differ only by what the overrides say; the manifest cannot verify that the real vehicles share what it claims they share, only that these designs do. Published figures are optional, and a family without them is a convenience rather than a measurement. pinned_family needs each variant to override boosters.n_total, and reports the ones that do not rather than guessing
Validity range / limitations: A family is the ONE configuration where the shared-core limitation of ACCURACY 6b.3 is checkable instead of arguable, because the variants fly one core and each publishes its own figure. The two measurements err in OPPOSITE directions - sized alone the small variants are 7 to 24 % too light, pinned they get 20 to 52 % too much payload - and both come from the same cause: this tool never carries a core oversized for the mission being flown. Requiring published figures to be marked reference is what stops a validation set grading itself against its own guesses
Implementation: families.discover / find / load_manifest / size_family / pinned_family, CLI 'family', GUI /api/families and the Architecture & families tab
Verification: tests/test_families.py: discovery, five kinds of malformed manifest refused by name, the A62-as-overrides reproducing the shipped ariane62.yaml to 1e-9, and both measurement directions pinned with their signs asserted

Calculation / model: Pinned architecture trade: payload against strap-on count
Mathematical formulation: hold every stage's loaded propellant, dry mass, start-up and unusable split, effective Isp and mass flow, and the strap-on UNIT design, at a converged design's values; change only the count; re-solve the parallel burn with boosters.phase_sequence rather than carrying the reference design's stored parallel-phase term; bisect the payload for dv_achieved = dv_required(orbit); refuse a count whose lift-off T/W <= 1
Inputs [units]: a converged result, a booster count
Outputs [units]: payload [kg], GLOM [kg], lift-off T/W, per-stage delta-v
Reference (verified): Book Sec. 3.8 pp.195-197 (performance curves) and Fig. 5.21 (parallel-burn phasing); the pinning itself is SUPPLEMENTARY
Assumptions: The stages are not re-sized or re-optimised: tankage, engine count, avionics and fairing stay as sized for the reference mission. Ascent time is held at the reference design's value, so the extra gravity loss a thrust-starved configuration really pays is not charged to it. An air-lit group needs a ground-lit group below it to ignite it, so a count with no ground-lit boosters is refused rather than flown
Validity range / limitations: FrozenVehicle carries the parallel phase as ONE stored number - on Ariane 64 about -2,900 m/s, a bookkeeping correction between the serial rocket equation and the phase model, not a contribution. That number is a property of the reference booster count, so holding it fixed while changing the count is exactly the assumption the trade invalidates. Measured against the two families that publish figures for several counts of one core (Delta II 73xx/74xx/79xx, Ariane 62/64), pinning over-predicts the smaller variant by 19-52 % and the payload-vs-count slope is 19-34 % too shallow; the bias is printed beside every sweep and deliberately not corrected, because R32 already measured that fitted loss corrections do not survive leave-one-out
Implementation: architecture.pin / PinnedVehicle.with_boosters / payload_for_architecture / booster_count_sweep / core_for_boosters, CLI 'architecture'
Verification: tests/test_architecture.py: six designs reproduce the sizing loop's per-stage delta-v to 1e-9, the same GLOM and T/W, and the payload root-find returns the design payload to 0.5 %; the published cross-family bias is pinned one-sided so a sign flip fails; T/W <= 1 and boosters outlasting the core's propellant are asserted to refuse rather than answer

Calculation / model: Zero-lift drag coefficient built up from the vehicle's geometry
Mathematical formulation: Cd = Cd_friction + Cd_forebody + Cd_boattail + Cd_base on Sref, per body, summed over the core and attached strap-ons. Friction: Cf = 1/(1.50 ln Re - 5.6)^2, or 0.032 (Rs/L)^0.2 above Re_crit = 51 (Rs/L)^-1.039; x (1 - 0.1 M^2) subsonic, / (1 + 0.15 M^2)^0.58 supersonic; Cd = Cf (1 + 1/(2 fB)) A_wet/Sref. Cone or flare of half-angle eps on its own annulus: 2.1 sin^2(eps) + 0.5 sin(eps)/sqrt(M^2 - 1) for M >= 1.3; sin(eps) with slope 4/(gamma+1) (1 - 0.5 Cd) at M = 1; a cubic between; 0.8 sin^2(phi) + a M^b below. Blunt tip: Cd_sharp (Sref - S_tip)/Sref + Cd_hemisphere S_tip/Sref. Base: 0.12 + 0.13 M^2 (M < 1), 0.25/M (M > 1), on the base area less the nozzle exit area while thrusting. Boattail: base drag on the removed annulus x {1, (3 - g)/2, 0} for g = l/(d1 - d2) below 1, 1 to 3, above 3
Inputs [units]: sized geometry (segment lengths and diameters), strap-on count and geometry, nozzle exit areas, Mach number, altitude, surface roughness [m], nose shape, nose bluntness
Reference (verified): NOT a book method: the book gives none and points to Missile DATCOM (Sec. 6.4.1, p.358). Base and blunt-nose drag: Fleeman, Tactical Missile Design, AIAA 2001, p.23 (Fig. 2.7) and p.24 (Fig. 2.8), read in the owner's copy. Friction, conical forebody, flare and boattail relations: OpenRocket technical documentation (S. Niskanen, for OpenRocket 1.1.6, 2011), Sec. 3.4.2, 3.4.3, 3.4.5 and Appendix B.2, read in its LaTeX source; that document attributes them to Barrowman (1967) and Hoerner (1965), which were NOT read
Assumptions: Turbulent boundary layer from the nose; Reynolds number on body length with US76 density and Sutherland viscosity; a tangent ogive takes the cone's value at and above Mach 1; the cubic between Mach 1 and 1.3 and the linear blend of the two friction corrections across Mach 0.9-1.1 are this tool's, where the source leaves the form open; zero angle of attack; one shape per flight phase, all on the lift-off reference area
Validity range / limitations: No protuberances, fins or engine fairings; no interference between a core and its strap-ons; no plume effect beyond filling the nozzle exit area; circular sections only. Measured (docs/DRAG.md): -6 % against the Saturn V's measured axial force at max-q; mean absolute error 18 % against the Vanguard wind-tunnel curve of book Fig. 6.10, high in the transonic onset; 35 % high against the book's Titan II curve of Fig. 6.13, which falls below what a blunted re-entry vehicle's pressure drag alone allows. Depends on the nose length, which most designs here carry as an ASSUMED input
Implementation: drag_buildup.Configuration / configuration_from_result; aerodynamics.geometry_model; trajectory.ascent_vehicle_from_result (one shape per burn) and trajectory.drag_table; default of mission.aerodynamics.drag_model

Calculation / model: Orbit reached at the end of the flight, and the events timeline
Mathematical formulation: Inertial horizontal speed V = v_site sin(beta) + sqrt((v cos gamma)^2 - (v_site cos beta)^2), vertical speed v sin(gamma) unchanged; eps = v_i^2/2 - mu/r; a = -mu/(2 eps); h = r V; e = sqrt(1 + 2 eps h^2/mu^2); r_p = a(1 - e), r_a = a(1 + e); mu = g0 Rp^2. Reached if both apsides are within max(10 km, 2 %) below the target or above it; otherwise in orbit if the perigee is above 100 km; otherwise not in orbit. Timeline: the integration's logged events plus Mach 1, maximum dynamic pressure and peak acceleration read from the recorded history
Inputs [units]: burnout speed [m/s], flight path angle [deg] and altitude [m] relative to the launch site; launch-site speed [m/s] and launch azimuth [deg] from the delta-v budget; target perigee and apogee altitude [m]
Outputs [units]: perigee and apogee altitude [m], eccentricity, inertial speed [m/s] and flight path angle [deg], a verdict; a list of events
Reference (verified): Standard two-body relations (energy and angular momentum); NOT located as a method in the book. The launch-site speed is added back by inverting the vector subtraction the delta-v budget already makes (M05). The 100 km floor and the 10 km / 2 % tolerance are this tool's reporting thresholds and come from no source
Assumptions: Two-body motion after the last burn. A flight of M108 carries its own inertial speed, because it is integrated on a turning Earth; for any other state the launch site's speed is added back. Not checked when the ascent is stopped before the last stage
Validity range / limitations: No J2, no drag after burnout, no plane change. The thresholds are ASSUMED and looser than a real injection accuracy. A solid last stage cannot be cut off, so its surplus shows as an apogee above the target
Implementation: trajectory.insertion_orbit / trajectory.timeline; set on TrajectoryResult.insertion by fly_design; shown in the Trajectory tab, the Summary tab and the report
Verification: tests/test_trajectory.py: a level burnout at circular speed gives a circular orbit at that altitude; a speed surplus puts the burnout point at perigee and a deficit at apogee, the surplus checked against vis-viva; the three verdicts; the launch-site speed inverts orbit.needed_speed at three azimuths; the timeline is in time order and its max-q and Mach 1 rows agree with the history

Calculation / model: Ascent to orbit: steering, cutoff, coast and restart on a turning Earth
Mathematical formulation: M63's equations with w = omega cos(i): dv/dt = (T cos(a) cos(yaw) - D)/m - (g - w^2 r) sin(gamma); v dgamma/dt = T sin(a) cos(yaw)/m - (g - w^2 r - v^2/r) cos(gamma) + 2 w v. Vertical rise, pitch kick, gravity turn to 60 km or 1 kPa; then linear tangent steering tan(theta) = A + (B - A) t/tf above the local horizon, with A and B solved (damped Newton) for the insertion altitude and a level arrival. Cutoff when the orbital energy equals the target orbit's. Insertion directly up to 200 km; above that at a parking altitude on an ellipse reaching the target, a coast to the apoapsis and a level second burn; a high apogee from a circular parking orbit, burning along the velocity at the next equator crossing. A solid last stage fires once, level, after a coast to near the top. Yaw: sin(yaw) = (site speed across the orbit plane)/(vacuum ideal speed). Throttle = min(1, a_max m g0/T) down to the engine's minimum. The pitch kick is the one that leaves the most speed in hand
Inputs [units]: sized vehicle (masses, thrusts, exit areas), drag model, atmosphere, orbit, launch site, limits
Outputs [units]: state history, losses, speed in hand [m/s], propellant left [kg], orbit reached
Reference (verified): Linear tangent steering Eq. 6:59, p.371, and its terminal conditions p.372; how to fly to each altitude pp.372-373 and Fig. 6.20; air-launch initial conditions p.372; gravity turn Sec. 6.4.7; equations Table 6.1
Source class: Book (steering law, equations, ways to orbit) + SUPPLEMENTARY (rotating-frame terms, yaw, the solver, the search for the kick)
Assumptions: Point mass in the orbit plane; no wind, no lift (an air launch is pulled up by its thrust instead of its wing), no attitude dynamics. ASSUMED: hand-over 60 km or 1 kPa, parking altitude 185 km, kick not before 30 m/s, 3 m/s charged per kPa of dynamic pressure over the design's limit. Every liquid last stage can stop and restart once, with no propellant lost in between
Validity range / limitations: Not an optimal-control solution: one kick and one linear tangent arc. Tried against the inertial-frame version of the law (2 m/s at most) and, for solids, a free pitch slope (1 m/s). No plane change and no apogee burn for a geostationary orbit. An upper stage that falls faster than it gains speed has no solution, and the flight says so. Constant thrust: real cores that throttle or shut an engine down fly on their full thrust unless given a minimum throttle and an acceleration limit
Verification: tests/test_ascent.py: a coast keeps its inertial energy and angular momentum to 1e-7; losses close to 1e-6 m/s; level arrival at the insertion altitude; second burn equal to the Hohmann value; no neighbouring kick does better. Against reality (tools/validate_ascent.py, docs/ASCENT_VALIDATION.md): 16 real vehicles flown on their published masses, and the book's Pegasus and Saturn V flights

Calculation / model: Ascent losses from the vehicle's own simulated flight (loss model 'simulated')
Mathematical formulation: fixed point: size with loss L; fly (M108); L' = (dv_required - orbital speed lines) - speed in hand; repeat with a secant until |L' - L| < 1 m/s. In the split optimiser: losses flown at 9 or 11 splits, interpolated with a thin-plate spline, flown again at each optimum until the two agree within 10 m/s
Outputs [units]: ascent loss [m/s] in the delta-v budget
Reference (verified): No book method: the book loss models are regressions (M37 and its simpler siblings)
Assumptions: Off unless chosen. At the fixed point the vehicle reaches its orbit with exactly its margin and allowance lines left. Monte-Carlo holds the nominal losses
Validity range / limitations: Where the ascent does not close there is nothing to size with, and the sizing is refused with the reason. Removes the regression's margin of safety as well as its error: every other optimism of the model goes straight into the mass. docs/ASCENT.md has the measurement on the 24 validation vehicles
Verification: tests/test_ascent.py: the sized vehicle arrives with nothing to spare; the split search moves with the losses; refusal with a way out
